enonce_markdown: The Nile is traditionally regarded as the longest river in the world, flowing northward for roughly 6,650 kilometres through eleven African countries before its waters finally reach the sea. Name the sea into which the Nile empties, and name the African country where this happens.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A general-knowledge question about physical geography is answered by recalling a well-established fact — here, the identity and course of a major world river — rather than by guessing. When a question names a landmark and asks where it leads, picture its route on a map before answering.

### Answer

The Nile empties into the **Mediterranean Sea**, through its delta on the northern coast of **Egypt**. Along its course, the river also flows through countries such as Uganda, South Sudan, Sudan and Ethiopia, but Egypt is where it finally reaches the sea.

enonce_markdown: In March 1957, one African country made history by becoming the first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence from colonial rule. It was led at the time by a Prime Minister who would later become its first President. Which country was it?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A multiple-choice general-knowledge question is best answered by matching the precise details given — here, the exact year and the political role described — to the one option that fits all of them, rather than picking the first vaguely familiar name.

### Answer

**A) Ghana.** Formerly known as the Gold Coast under British colonial rule, Ghana gained independence on 6 March 1957 under the leadership of Kwame Nkrumah, who served first as Prime Minister and later became the country's first President when Ghana became a republic in 1960.

enonce_markdown: A South African political leader spent 27 years in prison for opposing the apartheid system before being released in February 1990. Four years later, following his country's first fully democratic elections, he became its first Black President. Name this leader and give the year he became President.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A biographical general-knowledge question is answered by linking a person to specific, verifiable milestones — dates, roles, achievements — rather than a vague impression of who they were. Work out the answer step by step from the clues given: here, the length of imprisonment and the timing of the release point to one clearly identifiable figure.

### Answer

The leader is **Nelson Mandela**. He was released from prison on 11 February 1990 and became **President of South Africa in 1994**, after South Africa's first elections open to all races. He had also been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993, jointly with then President F. W. de Klerk, for their work in ending apartheid.

enonce_markdown: A present-day African country takes its official name directly from a set of impressive stone ruins found within its own borders. This fortified city was built without mortar by the ancestors of the Shona people between roughly the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, and once served as the capital of a powerful trading kingdom. Name the country and the ruins that gave it its name.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A question about cultural or archaeological heritage is answered by recalling the historical facts attached to a specific site — who built it, when, and what it later came to symbolise — rather than by describing what a ruin might generally look like.

### Answer

The country is **Zimbabwe**, and the ruins are known as **Great Zimbabwe** (from the Shona word meaning "stone houses"). Built by the ancestors of the Shona people and flourishing between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a powerful trading kingdom, and it is from this site that the modern country took its name upon independence in 1980.

enonce_markdown: The African Union is the continental body that succeeded the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) in 2002. It has its permanent headquarters in one particular city. In which city is the African Union headquartered?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A question about an international institution is answered by recalling a specific, factual detail about that institution — such as its seat or headquarters — rather than assuming it must sit in the continent's largest or best-known city.

### Answer

**A) Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.** The African Union has been headquartered there since its founding in 2002, when it replaced the Organisation of African Unity, which had itself been founded in 1963.

enonce_markdown: In 2010, a major international football tournament was staged on African soil for the very first time in its history. Name the country that hosted this tournament, and name the country whose national team won the final.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A higher-difficulty general-knowledge question often asks for two linked facts rather than one — here, the host and the eventual winner of the same event — so both parts must be recalled accurately and correctly matched to one another, not just one detail in isolation.

### Answer

**South Africa** hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup, the first ever held on the African continent. In the final, played at Soccer City in Johannesburg, **Spain** defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time to win its first World Cup title.
